"Yes. He—or she—came on a mat-
ter of business. What I said about a
teacher was mere nonsense. Now you
know the whole thing."


"Excepting what the business was,"
Margaret said incredulously.


"The business was an uncut stone,"
answered Logotheti with indifference.
He had one to sell, and I bought it.
He was recommended to me by a man
in Constantinople. He came to Mar-
settles on French steamer with two
Greek merchants who were coming to
Paris, and they brought him to my
door. That is the whole story. And
here is the ruby. I bought it for you,
because you like those things. Will
you take it?"


He held out what looked like a little
ball of white tissue paper, but Marga-
ret turned her face from him.


"You treat me like a child," she
said.


To her own great surprise and indign.
ation, her voice was unsteady and
she felt something burning in her
eyes. She was almost frightened at
the thought that she might be going
to cry, out of sheer modification.


Logotheti said nothing for a
moment. He began to unroll the paper
from the precious stone, but changed
his mind, wrapped it up again, and
put it back into his watch-pocket be-
fore he spoke.


"I did not mean it as you think," he
said softly.


She turned her eyes without moving
her head, till she could just see that
he was leaning forward, resting his
wrists on his knees, bending his head
and apparently looking down at his
loosely hanging hands. His attitude
expressed detection and disappoint-
ment. She was glad of it. He had no
right to think that he could make her
as angry as she still was, angry even
to tears, and then bribe her to smile
again when he was tired of teasing
her. Her eyes turned away again, and
she did not answer him.


"I make mistakes sometimes," he
said, speaking still lower, "I know
I do. When I am with you I cannot be
always thinking of what I say. It's
too much to ask, when a man is as far
gone as I am."


"I should like to believe that," Mar-
garet said, without looking at him.


"Is it hard to believe?" he asked so
gently that she only just heard the
words.


"You don't make it easy, you know,"
said she with little defiance, for she
felt that she was going to yield before
long.


"I don't know how to. You're not
in the least capricious—and yet."


"You're mistaken," Margaret an-
swered, turning to him suddenly. "I'm
the most capricious woman in the
world! Yesterday I wrote a long let-
ter to a friend, and then I suddenly
tore it up—there were ever so many
pages! I daresay that if I had writ-
ten just the same letter this morning
I should have sent it. If that is not
caprice, what is it?"


"It may have been wisdom to tear
it up," Logotheti suggested.

Indianapolis.—Thirty cases of typhoid fever have baffled the health officials of Thorntown; there are at least thirty cases at Newcastle and epidemics are threatened in various other parts of the state. The department of foods and drugs of the state board of health has sent out 81 containers for water, issued on request, as means of shipping water samples to the department for analysis. But three containers are in the office and there are 20 requests for containers on file, received from various parts of Indiana.

"The trouble is, persons who attribute typhoid fever to the condition of the water used for drinking purposes are frequently mistaken," said H. T. Barnard, state food and drug commissioner. "The real trouble more frequently lies in the proximity of surface vaults to seats of infection.

"We have made repeated analyses of water in the laboratory to fix the cause of typhoid epidemics, and in many cases we have failed to find anything wrong. Personal inspections have revealed the cause of the disease, and the up-ground vault is, in many instances, held responsible.

Many cities have excellent sewer systems, for which they have paid immense amounts of money, but the people do not use them. There are 1900 vaults in Indianapolis, and probably 1,000 are within the reach of a sewer. Greensburg has 400 or 500 open vaults with one of the best sewer systems in the state. The city was bonded for $4,000 a few years ago to establish the sewers, but the people so far have not recognized the fact that it was constructed to be used. Some one ought to write a tract on 'The Value of Utilized Sewer.'

Monaghan as chairman of the meeting, and Mr. Monaghan will then present Mr. Redmond. Following the latter's address, Miss Margaret Troy will render vocal solo. An address by the Rev. M. Stritch, S. J., of Detroit College, will complete the program. His topic will be "The Irish cause."

No admission will be charged for the Redmond lecture, but collection will be taken and donations to the home rule cause will be received in any amount. Bishop Williams, it is announced, will attend the meeting in company with Bishop Foley.

Ex-Governor Napoleon B. and disastrous wreck on the Pennsyl-
vania railroad, resulting in the death
Of a locomotive engineer and two
firemen and the injury of three other
trainmen occurred this afternoon at
Thirtieth street near the Western
limits of this city. The dead are:
Engineer D. H. Rorabaugh, Cone
maugh, Pa; Fireman Ira Reed, Pitts
burg; and Fireman A. c. Furlong,
Conemaugh, Pa.


The injured are at the Altoona hos
pital. A fast freight train westbound
was just starting up the mountain,
helped in the rear by two locomotives
when the boiler of the second Of the
rear engines exploded. The boiler
rose from the engine frame and was
hurled through the air just an ex-
press train composed entirely of ex-

along on the next track. The express

cmbankment 800 feet from where 1t

wreckage and crushed under the ten

train engine No. 2416, of which he

ined the exploded boiler declared that

ter.

freight train, being stopped only
short distance away.

We would emphasize the fact that every farm where cotton is planted has some plants just at this time bearing at the rate of over a bale to the acre, it makes no reference how poor the yield may average. This is a fact and not fancy. Therefore, whatever variety you have, if you do not expect to buy stock seed next year, or if you expect to plant next spring seed that are gathered from your own farm this fall, see to it that you get the best your field contains for this purpose, and then select from the best use as seed for pet patch.


THE PLANT.


In order to be sure of getting in your selection a uniform type of plants, make a typical plant that conforms well to the variety type you are planting. To do this, go to the best part of the field where the cotton is good. See that the plant you are to select has not less than 3 to 5 bolls, more would be better. From now on until after the Kansas game, the Cornhusker squad will have the longest, hardest practice of the season. The men will be kept on the jump until darkness prevents further work and there will be no easing up.

In the matter of the distribution of game birds in Missouri, it appears that State Warden Jesse A. Tolerton has been making good. The Republic has information from many sources that the birds, more particularly English pheasants, which he placed a few months ago, have propagated finely, and will continue to multiply if not disturbed by hunters.

Warden Tolerton has been particularly delighted with the success of the birds which, under the direction of Doctor Will, were placed at the reservation just north of Jefferson Barracks.

He is about to send to the Commandant a considerable bunch of Hungarian partridges, which, the Warden believes, will breed much better in this climate than the pheasants.

The Warden expresses himself in a letter to The Republic as being much pleased with the fact that the officers of the army have taken this matter up in true sportsmanlike way, and will give all the encouragement they can to the project.

S. W. Lyons, of Fulton, has said in a letter to the Game and Fish Commissioner, which the latter has transmitted to The Republic, that, notwithstanding all the difficulties he has encountered, he is now about to make success of the planting in his environment of some English pheasants, sent to him a few months ago.

According to Mr. Lyons' letter, the fecundity of these birds is wonderful. He found ninety eggs as the product of his small allotment during the course of his connection with his attempt, which only now has begun to be flourishing, according to his letter.

He says Missouri-born English pheasants will come and eat out of his hand; that the tame young chicks are just like ordinary young chickens and if the shot of the hunter can be prevented from sounding over them for the next two years, and if similar communities can be organized, Missouri will be filled with game birds of the first quality.

J. Atkinson, of the city engineers
department, lost his position because
he had testified to facts displeasing
to his superiors were made by Chair
man Lynch at the special committee
which is investigating conditions in
the office of the city engineer at a
meeting Tuesday night.

Mr. Atkinson was discharged by
First Assistant Engineer Jackson Boil-
ton on Tuesday morning. Mr. Bolton
said he had taken action because he
had found Mr. Atkinson absent from
his work on three occasions. The
discharged inspector admitted having
been absent, but declared that the
occurrences dated back several
months, since which time he had been
given other work by the city.

Mr. Adams of the committee, asked
Mr. Bolton why he had not dis-
charged Mr. Atkinson at the time of
the offense. Evidence of unfair deal-
ing was apparent, he said, when the
inspector had been given another
sewer to build, only to be discharged
on old offense after he had given
judicial evidence.

not to be considered Mr. Atkinson a
competent employee. The city engi-
neer replied in the affirmative, al-
though he said he had been negli-
gent in inspecting work on Broad
street. Mr. Atkinson explained this
negligence with the statement

that he had been given three jobs
to look after at the same time.

Tells Of Sewer Troubles.

Mr. Atkinson made a lengthy state-
ment in which he described his work
in the city. He had been with the
engineer's department nine years, he
said. He described work on various
sewers where there had been trouble.
He dwelt at length on the Broad
street sewer which became choked,
thereby causing water to back out
instead of running through. No re-
port was made to the city engineer
regarding this choking. Mr. Atkinson
said he merely told Mr. Bolton at
the time that a head wall can be erected to hold the water
until the work was completed. Mr.
Bolton approved the suggestion, no
doubt, and the head wall was built.
Mr. Bolton denied this statement
and said he had never heard of such
a thing until the entire work was

near Leigh, where he had changed

correct and filed his notebook with

gineer's office for work then, and
he was told by Mr. Bolton that
he had better look for another job.

kinson and the questioning of Mr.
Bolton, Mr. Lynch left the chair and
announced the discharge of the in-
spector a piece of persecution on
part of Mr. Bolton. He said:
"You'd hate to see any man lose
his job for coming here and telling
the committee the truth. If there
had been any negligence it was on
part of Mr. Bolton for not dis-
charging this man when he was found
absent from his work, not holding
him until months afterwards

table to the engineer in charge of
work. It looks like persecution to

ond—the Interstate Commerce Com-

greater importance on its hands that

street railways the attention they need,
even if it had unquestioned authority
to do so.

commission, or a broadening of the
powers of the District Commis-
sioners over the street car companies. Such
indefinite provisions as those contain-

wiped off the books. In their place

providing just what the street car

the authority of the public utilities
commission or the District Commis-
sioners begins and just where it ends.

street railway control we are going

stone wall. Just as we've been butting

Alva, Okla., Sept. 13.—Arthur Cornish, a young man 22 years old, was arrested Sunday for the murder of Joe Vineyard, who was found covered with debris in his bed in an old dugout in which he had lived for years. Cornish has confessed to the killing and claims it was done in self-defense.

From his story a dramatic scene must have been enacted in the old man's hovel. Cornish had rented one of the dead man's farms and owed him five past due notes. While passing the dugout Cornish was called into the house by Vineyard and told he must raise the money. This Cornish consented to do, but told the old man that he proposed to have pay for the damage Vineyard's stock had done to his crops while allowed to run at large, which the old man would not consent to. This started a quarrel and Vineyard, Cornish says, tried to strike him with a club. Cornish parried the blow. The old man, he says, then threw clevis and missed, the weapon striking a post in the dugout, breaking into two pieces. This weapon the sheriff found and thus far Cornish's statement is corroborated.

The youth says he then pulled his revolver and shot the old man four times. He claims to have no recollection of having covered the body up and on his way from the house lost his revolver. The weapon was picked up by the neighbors and this was recognized as one that Cornish had tried to sell some time ago. This led to inquiry, and when interviewed by the officers Cornish confessed. The old hovel in which the man had lived shows that desperate battle had taken place. The stove was knocked down and one chair was broken, and there is no doubt in the minds of people who knew him that he would have killed the young man in the scuffle. While Vineyard has never been accused of assault or had any personal encounters, yet he was arrested at one time for misusing a girl in the neighborhood and was defended at that time by Jesse Dunn, who now is the chief justice of the supreme court, and was acquitted.

In October, 1909, the general council of Korean missionaries, assembled in Seoul, decided to pray and work for a million converts in Korea in a year's time.

This without doubt constitutes the most daring and courageous forward movement undertaken by any country in the history of the Christian church. And it is strangely significant that such a conquest should be attempted in a nation where the first mission was opened only a quarter of century ago; and where the people have had the New Testament in their own language for less than a score of years. The splendid faith of the Korean missionaries is seen even more since the number of church members and catechumens in the country is only about 10,000, and the total adherents about 100,000.

The great movement for a million souls originated in prayer and the study of God's word. About six months ago a little group of missionaries in Songdo felt keenly the need of more power in their own lives and in the lives of the Koreans around them. They met in fasting and prayer each day they studied God's word to find out how to pray. On the evening of the fourth day the meeting was prolonged until midnight, but three of the missionaries remained in prayer until 4 a. m. At that time God's Spirit descended upon them in power and they were filled with great peace and love, and an intense desire to pray through to victory.

A few days later these same three missionaries, Dr. W. T. Reid, Rev. J. Stokes and Rev. F. X. Gamble, met together for an entire day of prayer. Suddenly, as they prayed, the Holy Spirit seemed to fill the room, while Mr. Gamble seemed to see Christ standing over Korea with hands outstretched in blessing. Following this these three young men and two other Songdo missionaries spent several days in prayer in a temple on a nearby mountain and then went forth filled with a stunning passion for souls.

As Mr. Stokes went through the country villages he asked the Koreans in a certain district whether they would work and pray for 4,000 souls in a year. They went to work so willingly, that the matter of asking God for a great multitude of converts was brought up at the annual conference of the Methodist church, south, held in Seoul. They adopted as their watch-word for the ensuing year: "Two Hundred Thousand Souls for Christ."

Dr. Reid reported to the general council of evangelical missions the action of the Methodist body, and a committee was appointed to consider whether all the missions working in Korea ought not to unite in a similar plan. After prolonged prayer and careful consideration the committee recommended that all the missionary bodies should unite in asking God for a million souls the following year. The council after earnest prayer for guidance, adopted the plan, and thus was inaugurated the most remarkable gospel campaign in history; the attempt to Christianize in a year's time a million of the thirteen million inhabitants of that land.

in General Lee's report of January,
1864, that Stuart was instructed to
lose no time in placing his command
on the right of our column as soon as
he perceived the enemy moving north-
ward, with the orders he actually re-
ceived to accompany the column of
General Ewell. But is there any incon-
sistency? In using this language Lee
was thinking of his army as a unit,
and could not have meant that he ex-
pected Stuart to be with Longstreet
when he had ordered him to be with
Ewell, as is stated in the report which
Mosby criticizes. This is explicitly
shown one or two before the allusion to
"the right of our column." "Our column," in the
connection in which it stands, can only
mean General Ewell's column. Such
criticism is captious and unfair.

In analyzing Colonel Mosby's de-
tense of General Stuart, and pointing
out what I consider his mistakes, I
have had no desire to associate myself
with those who seek to cast the whole
responsibility for the failure of the
Gettysburg campaign on the shoulders
of the commander-in-chief of the
cavalry of the Army of Northern Vir-
ginia. General A. P. Hill, General
Ewell, General Longstreet—especially
the last—must all share it with him.

I think it must be acknowledged that
the battle was precipitated by the un-
authorized advance of General Hill on
July 1. I think also that Colonel
Mosby is right in the opinion that Lee
had no intention of fighting a general
battle at Gettysburg. He was dragged
into it by his lieutenant. But on the
other hand, I think that if General
Stuart had been with Early, as he might
and ought to have been, on the night
of the 30th, or the morning of the
30th, his cavalry would in all prob-
ability have prevented the rash adj-
vance of General Hill. Marching from
York to Cashtown on the 30th by way
of Heidlersburg he would have felt
the enemy, ascertained his position
and strength and left no excuse for
that reconnaissance which prematurely
brought on the battle on a field Lee
had not selected.

Colonel Mosby's book involves very
serious charges on General Lee,
which his soldiers are loath to accept
save on the most incontrovertible evi-
dence. He asks us to believe, as
I have said, that the report of the
Gettysburg campaign which General
Lee signed in January, 1864, not only
reflects gross injustice on General
Stuart, but bristles with inconsistent
facts and grievous mistakes on points
of capital importance. It is incredible
that these two reports of the battle
were signed by General Lee without
reading them. It is inconsistent with
his habit in other cases. We know that
he took time to read General Pickett's
report of the battle.

Why not then read his own report?
And if General Lee read them, then
certainly their salient statements, to
say the least, have the stamp of his
authority. But Colonel Mosby asserts
that it was not Lee's purpose on the
28th of June to advance against Har-
risburg, though he says so in his re-
port, and though Colonel Marshall says
he himself sent orders to that effect
to Hill and Longstreet on the night
of the 28th. He insists also that the
change of plan and the orders to con-
centrate at Cashtown were not the
consequence of the intelligence brought
by scout on June 28th, although Gen-
eral Lee affirms it in his report.
No matter: Colonel Mosby knows better.
He is sure that Lee had ordered Ewell
back from Carlisle on the 28th, and he
is satisfied by this by the letter in
Lee's letter-book, not copied, but writ-
ten from memory afterwards by Col-
onel Venable. His whole argument on
this point rests, as I have said, on
the accuracy of the date of that letter.
I have shown that on the hypothesis of
an error in date, the 28th instead of
the 30th, the inconsistencies Colonel
Mosby alleges disappear.

CHICAGO, May 17.-Shippers and
manufacturers of the United States are
today meeting in Chicago to voice a
protest against the threatened advance
in railroad rates. Approximately 400
individual shippers and $50 associa-
tions, each representing hundreds of
rate payers, are included in the meet
ing.


The delegates do not assume the
attitude that any advance in rates is
unreasonable, but take the position
that the increase that the railroads de-
clare is necessary by advancing wages
is not justifiable on the financial show
ing of the carriers and that no raise
should be made until the interstate
commerce commission has investigat-
ed.


An answer to telegram to Presi
dent McRhea of the Pennsylvania rail
road system, asking his position, is
anxiously awaited by the shippers to-
day.

foot were taken by the Methodist mis-

attended the Mission school. He was
one of the first Indians to be converted
and for many years he assisted in this
work. Times were hard in those days
and many time Joe used his canoe for
a tent, while travelling the shore line
from the 500 to Duluth.

Indians and was noted for his good,
honest adyice when consulted by his
brethren. He is survived by a wife,
who has resided with him at Silver
Creek for the past fifty years or more.


No date has been set for the funeral,
but it will probably take place tomor-
row afternoon, services being held at
the M. E. Mission, Rev. c. M. Merrill
officiating, assisted by Rev. T. C.
Thomas. Interment will be in the Pin
cry cemetery.

the law if he cut her tail, no matter
if she switched it sixty times a minute.


"If you had come home, Samuel—if
you had come home and made excuses,
but you didn't. You jest strolled in
as placid as if you had been out hoe
ing cabbages. You could have ex-
plained that one dog pitched into the
other without provocation and that
you didn't interfere because you were
afraid of being bit, but you just
wound up the clock and said it was
time to go to bed. That was deception
on top of crime. How do I know that
you won't smile on me and then chop
me up with the axe an hour later?"
Samuel didn't know any way she
could find out, and he didn't believe
there was case in point in the book
before him. It did, however, state
that striking a man with pitchfork
constituted much graver crime than
batting him with a long handled
shovel. Mrs. Dolby sobbed and wept.
Her tears fell on her alpaca dress and
on her satchel, and it was several min
utes before she rose up and said:


"Well, must be going. Little did I
think when married you, twenty
eight years ago, that tonight I'd have
to leave my own house because you
have turned pirate. Do you want to
say goodbye to me—"


Nothing from the deacon.
Separation and Return.
"Of course I shan't write to you."
The deacon didn't fall off his chair.
"And if you come to me on your
bended knees—"


The idea of his knees bending work
ed up a new emotion, and she leaned
against the door and sobbed. That
was fine reading the deacon had, and
he was deeply interested.


"It is night, and have got this
satchel to carry, but if I get afraid or
tuckered out I can sleep beside some
haystack."


The deacon never cracked a smile.
She opened the door, and he never
moved. She went, but he paid no heed,
Even when the door closed he took no
notice.


Mrs. Dolby went down the path and
leaned on the gate and looked back at
the house. No one came to the door to
call her back. She put down the satch-
el and gave it a kick. Her tears and
sobs ceased. Had the deacon tainted
away? Had he blown his head off?
She softly advanced to the door and
held her ear to it. No sound. Then
she opened it and looked in. Then she
entered the kitchen. Same deacon,
same attitude.


"Samuel, I was thinking that if
I went tonight you'd have to get your
own breakfast and you wouldn't re
member how much coffee to put in"


And she removed her shawl and hat,
put another stick of wood into the
stove and five minutes later was sing
ing "The Old oaken Bucket" and tak
ing solid comfort.

 In the nature of things such a de- eision was to be expected, and one need not be a "eentralizationistn to rejoice that the court has so held. If the United States is to carry out the purposes of the reclamation act, it is essential that it be empowered to do so effectively and in the public interest. The reclamation act espeei- ally authorizes the inclusion of pri- vate property within a reclamation district, and while the government cannot compel owners to contract to accept the water and pay the assess ments, it ought to be possible for it to acquire by condemnation what ever private property is essential to carrying out the project, even though the greater part of the land within the district is in private ownership.

 The theory that the reclamation act was passed in order to enable the government to dispose of public land has no foundation. The act was pass ed to permit the utilization of water when the outlay involved was too great for private enterprise, or where tn eprobable time before re- turns could be expected was too long to be attractive to investors.  In fact the most immediately use ful projects are those in which all land is in private ownership. They will usually be so situated as to bear without difficulty the cost of irrigation.

Rutland June 7.—It is now evident
that Rutland will have an isolation hos-
pital, before Fall. The question of build-
ing this hospital has been agitated for
some time in the city board of health
and the aldermen long ago took favor-

be finished at first but later it may
be completed for the use of nurses or for
other purposes.

OF electrostatlc experiments, the shuf-

The score does not indicate the relative merits of the teams for Nebraska should have triumphed by at least eighteen points. Fortune smiled upon the Jayhawkers and fumbling cost the Cornhuskers at least two touchdowns.

Hopelessly outclassed in every department of the game, the Jayhawkers battled with determination which was tribute to Kennedy. Thrown back to their ten-yard line five times, and with the ball three times within the five-yard line, the Jayhawkers' fighting spirit never wavered and Nebraska failed to cross the goal line. Two thousand Kansas rooters were brought to their feet by the gameness of the fight.

Wonderful Game.

Cole had a superior team in every respect. The Cornhuskers played a wonderful game on the offense, carrying the ball nearly four times as far as their opponents. The defense was so vigorous that Kansas could not make much headway; the Jayhawkers displayed some real football ability.

For few minutes at the opening of the third quarter the proteges of Kennedy outplayed Nebraska, but the advantage was short lived and Nebraska took the ball from their own fifteen-yard line to within striking distance of the Jayhawker goal in a series of rushes which startled the confused Jayhawkers with the versatility of the attack. The only touchdown of this game was made in the final quarter after a series of plunges and end runs. O. Frank was called upon to carry the ball six yards and before Kansas was aware that the Cornhusker had started, he had darted through the line, past Tommy Johnson and over the chalk line. Twice during the first quarter Nebraska carried the ball to the ten-yard line, but once a tumble and the second time penalties robbed Nebraska of the score.

In the Second Quarter.

Again in the second quarter Nebraska carried the ball close to the Kansas goal, but a tumble cost the touchdown.

The story of the game is easily told in the statistics of yards gained on straight football and punts returned.

Nebraska gained 40 yards as against seventy-three for Kansas. In returning punts Nebraska made 100 yards and Kansas made two yards. The work of Chauner for Nebraska in going down under punts was easily as brilliant as has ever been seen in a Kansas field. He tackled fiercely. While the Nebraska defense was so stiff that Kansas had no chance to score.

Nebraska was thrown for loss of forty yards.

Nebraska offense was a whirlwind. Warner confused the Jayhawkers with a remarkable versatility in directing the Cornhusker attack. Around Warner Rathbone, Minor and Frank, Cole had developed a series of plays well calculated to dismay the Jayhawkers.

To the Editor of The Times dispatch;

Why, please, should the writer so incontinently be dubbed a sniat Correspondent, of the News, when his task consisted in calling the attention of that journal to the fact, undoubtedly known to it, but overlooked in its own editorial comment on the city's growth in the past decade, that part of that increase was due to the addition of Manchester? This is a fact that cannot be contravened, and as it seems to have been so questionable to you, it was written merely in the interests of accuracy and not at all with the idea of suggesting that Richmond's growth was not, in any case, as significant. Webster says that to moderate means to limit or reduce in extent or degree; to moderate; to qualify; to lower; so that the word, in this case, is used incorrectly. Since surely the increase when Manchester's inclusion is considered is not as astonishing as the same increase would have been had Manchester grown on its own, it is an expression which seems to express precisely the opinion of some of the residents of the latter place.

When all is said, your view of Richmond seems to be exaggerated. An increase of 15 per cent. would not make its population now vastly post tagging souls, while in the exact statement of the entire population, including Manchester, is so.

I am grateful for the many courtesies and great hospitality extended to me in Richmond! I would be very quick to respond to any accusation, even were I so inclined, when I am not. My recollections of it and its people are wholly delightful and I have and believe such will always be. I am sure this is a reasonable opinion of the city and its pride in their great commonwealth, contained in your editorial published yesterday in the press of Vir. under the caption of "Exaggeration"!

Here's to you. In the words of an old toast: "May you live ninety years and grow to enormous intelligence."

Very truly yours,

New York, October 10.

There is virtually no chance that the Democrats will obtain control of the senate as a result of next winter's elections. Aldrich Sure to Come Back.

New York will choose a senator to succeed Chauncey M. Depew. Mr. Depew wants to succeed himself, but it may be that certain passages in the senator's life few years ago will prevent his party from sending him back to the upper house.

To Fill up West Point.

The members of the fourth or as it is called, the plebe class, have just reported for admission to the United States Military academy at West Point. There are only 105 members of the class, and there still will be ten vacancies in the corps of cadets.

The committee on military affairs of the United States senate has just recommended a change in the law regulating appointments to West Point. The hope of the senators is to keep the ranks of the cadets full and to obviate the necessity of appointing every year to commissioned rank civil men who know little or nothing about the military service, and who have to be trained for several years before they are competent to command regular troops.

The authorized number of cadets at the military academy is 500, but the actual number in attendance at the school falls far below this mark, the deficiency being due to the fact that there are always existing vacancies caused by the failure of candidates to report or to pass the entrance examinations, or by the elimination of cadets who are found deficient in their studies or their conduct.

WASHINGTON, June 6.—Conservation legislation in the senate and the postal savings bill in the house constitute the feature of the congressional program for the coming week. The general opinion is that both measures will be voted upon before Saturday night and that they will be sent to conference.

Party lines will be dissolved and new lines of insurgency developed in the senate in connection with the public land withdrawal bill, which, it is expected, will be taken up to-morrow. Some of the western members are preparing to make vigorous assaults upon the Roosevelt-Garfield administration of the domain and as regards the blanket withdrawals of large areas.

It is not improbable this course will lead to some bitter criticism of the more conservative policies of the Ballinger administration.

Western Men in Rival Camps.

The discussions will be over the administration bill that has passed the house to authorize the president to withdraw public lands for purposes of classification for the protection of water power sites, for forest reserves, and to prevent mineral lands from falling into the hands of monopolies. Many western members, notably Senators Warren and Clark of Wyoming, Hepburn and Borah of Idaho, Carter of Montana and Hughes of Colorado, express fear that the enactment of this measure would mark the return of the policy of locking up great tracts of land and that the western states might be deprived of the benefits that would accrue from their development.

On the other hand, the more radical program carried out during the regime of former Chief Forester Pinchot is favored by such western members as Senators Dixon of Montana, Flint and Perkins of California, Piles of Washington, Chamberlain of Oregon and Bourne of Oregon, Smoot and Sutherland of Utah and numerous others.

Strong Support for Taft Plans.

Administration leaders are committed to the conservation legislation advocated by President Taft, and it is not doubted that the house bill for the withdrawal of public lands for conservation purposes will be passed at an early date and that the measure will emerge successfully from conference.

Statehood Legislation.

Supporters of statehood legislation are willing to give the administration measures the right of way. If the Republican leaders will give their pledge that a vote will be taken on the Arizona-New Mexico statehood bill it will be granted.

It is expected the committee on rules will meet on Tuesday and report out said rule that the statehood bill will be given the right of way through legislative channels. This rule will precipitate hot fight in the rules committee and on the floor of the house it is expected. Both of these committees were ordered by majority of the Republican caucus to take the action outlined.

Republican leaders in the house say there will be no fight. If putting the bill through without amendment, Democratic members of the house have made no promises, but in formal discussions have indicated that the vote will be along party lines except for the limited number of insurgent republicans who refused to be bound by their party caucus.

Unless some arrangement is reached by which conference can be avoided, both the house and the senate will name conferees on the railroad bill tomorrow.

To the Editor:-I was much interested in a description I read recently of the new method of planting adopted by some English growers that of ramming the roots into small openings like setting fence posts. Is not this about the same as the Stringfellow method, of which I know but little? P. C.

The method referred to is almost the same as the Stringfellow method. Mr. Stringfellow believes in the following: Prune the tree very closely at both top and root.

Make openings only large enough to take in the root, and pack the soil firmly by tramping with the foot, or even ramming with round-headed stick.

Prune very sparingly, if any, until the trees come into the first, or even second years, bearing enough to keep the tree in decent form.

When this method was first advocated by Mr. Stringfellow, Texas grower, it was received with little favor by practical orchardists, some of them even ridiculing the idea, saying that jamming the soil tightly about the roots would prevent growth. However, numerous experiments which have been conducted along this line the past few years show that the method has considerable merit, after all.

Most good orchardists now believe in trimming the roots very closely, and there is no doubt that it is much better to cut the tops back very vigorously rather than to plant them just as they come from the nursery.

Ithaca.—John D. Rockefeller's philanthropic scheme, which the Rockefeller foundation bill, now pending in congress, proposes to incorporate, was commended by President Jacob G. Schurman in an address before the Cornell congress Friday night. In summing up an exhaustive discussion of the measure, President Schurman said:

"I recognize that section No. of the bill, which defines the object of the Rockefeller foundation, authorizes and empowers that foundation to do anything and everything which may promote and advance human civilization, that is to say, morals and religion, art and science, manners and social intercourse, and all that concerns the political, economic, and material well being of individuals and communities. His ideas and organizing skill are adequate guarantees that he will carry out his scheme wisely and successfully, with incalculable benefit and blessing to mankind. It is in the interest of the nation that he be given free hand in the exercise of his colossal beneficence. So long as he is active it is safe to give the foundation the sort of organization he desires. Neither now nor hereafter does it seem necessary to limit the scope of his beneficence, which is coextensive with the efforts of mankind to attain higher civilization.

The only change I would desire to see in the proposed bill is the total or partial elimination of the method of selecting trustees by corporation. The organization might well be left a close corporation, if Mr. Rockefeller so desires, for a generation. But after that time I am confident that it would inure both to the efficiency of the foundation and to the public welfare—to say nothing of the satisfaction of the sentiment of democracy—if the majority of the trustees were appointed by the president of the United States, with the advice and consent of the senate, or selected by some other high abiding governmental agencies that may fairly be regarded as representing the people of the United States, whose welfare is the primary object of the immense and glorious benefaction."

"Mr. Cresson Ingle," hazarded, "is he an old, new friend of your cousins? I think he was not above the horizon when he went to Capri two years ago."

"He wants Elizabeth," she returned, adding quietly, "as you've seen." And when I had verified this assumption with a monosyllable she continued, "He's available but should hate to have it happen. He's hard."

"He seems to me much of a type with these others," said I.

"I suppose she finished her investigations. You told her all you could?"

"Almost."

"I suppose you wouldn't trust me with the reservation," she asked, smiling.

"I would trust you with anything," I answered seriously.

"You didn't crafty that child?" she said, half laughing. Then, to my surprise, she began again in a hurried low voice, "You didn't tell her—" and stopped there, breathless and troubled, letting me see that I had been right after all. This was what she wanted to talk about.

Mohammedans of India are very superstitious. No Mohammedan will take a bath on Sunday or Tuesday. But if one bathes on Wednesday all misfortunes and misery that are in store for him till the next Wednesday will be averted. As a rule, all Mohammedans bathe on Fridays before going to perform the jumma prayers. For donning new clothes Saturday, Sunday and Tuesday are regarded as bad days. If any one dons new dress or puts on new cloth or allows his tailor to cut piece of cloth on these days, he will live a miserable life till that dress or cloth gets torn or is thrown away. If a shirt is torn and if the wearer wants to stitch it, it must be taken off, for if it is stitched while on the body the person will soon die. Mohammedans will never allow barber to come near him on Tuesdays, for Tuesdays and Saturdays and Sundays are bad days for shaving. If absolutely necessary he will get himself shaved on Saturday or Sunday, but never on Tuesday, as his star is supposed to fall in blood if he does so. If one receives money or some valuable thing, it is taken with the right hand, for if it is taken with the left the person receiving it is said to forget all about it very soon or to mislay it. A devout Mohammedan will not start on a journey on Wednesday, for it is believed he will never return home safely if he does so. And it is said that even a snake never ventures out of its hole on this day.

As a result approximately 800 men are the owners or partial owners of homes in Mena.

Mining is now being worked on the property, but the force will be increased, ventilation systems improved and out and extraction of ore facilitated by the increase in stopping area. Mining is being worked on the new shaft.

There is there where the formation shows up in pits, the main formation being perhaps much more like and some of it with very odd colors, similar to those in the main part of the Goldfield district. It is probably true that the wealth producers to-day are being more fairly compensated for what they produce than ever before in the history of the country, and that necessarily makes the cost of living higher than ever before, because we live on what the wealth producers create. If the Republican party is responsible for this crime, then it glories in its achievements.

There are but three classes of people in our country and in the world, who have or can make any just complaint against what is known as the high cost of living. They are the office-holders and the salaried clerks, and the money-changers. If the office-holder is dissatisfied with his salary, the country can no doubt dispense with some of them or find a better substitute. I do not mean by this that I am in favor of low salaries, because I believe that every efficient public official should be honestly and justly compensated for his services, and when the wealth-producer is prosperous the country can afford to increase such wages where justice requires it. The same is true as to the salaried clerks, and already wages are being advanced from one end of the country to the other, to the greater or less degree, in proportion to the increased prosperity of the country. As for the money-changers, we leave Mr. Pou and his party to concern themselves about them.

My colleague next complains that I should call attention to and dilate upon the prosperity of this country and claim that the policies of the Republican party had any connection herewith. In reply, I want to ask that if the Republican party and its policies deserve no credit to any of the progress and development of this country, then what party deserves the credit? Does he claim that the Democratic party is in any way responsible for it?

He next complains that I should allude to the hard times that this country suffered under the last Democratic administration, and when I plainly deny that the Democratic party was in any way responsible for those conditions. In reply, if the Democratic party was not responsible, then who was? Mr. Pou seems to be aggrieved because the country always is more prosperous when the Republican party is in power than when the Democratic party is in power; he should not think that a friend would want to admit that Providence and the Republican party were in partnership.

No, Mr. Chairman, the fact is that the Republican party stands for great progressive and constructive American principles and ideas. It is the policies of the Republican party that has made this the greatest, the richest, the most powerful country in the world to-day. Here we have not only the greatest prosperity for each citizen, but the greatest liberty and the greatest voice and power in government.

And every poor-paid laborer in the world to-day, and every down-trodden human being who is hungry for a larger measure of liberty and the comforts of life, has his eye turned longingly toward the shores of America. They are not only yearning to come by the thousands and ten of thousands and millions, and they do come as fast as we will receive them. Ten times more would come if we would let down the barriers. It is the Republican party which has created the prosperous conditions which makes them want to come, and it is also the Republican party which has put up the bars to keep out those who are undesirable. Mr. Pou and his party declare that these people are coming to America to be robbed item by item by the Republican protective tariff, and the Republican trusts and monopolies have their liberties abridged.

TUCSON, Ariz., July 25.—After getting out its ninth weekly issue, the Voice of the People, the official organ of the newly-formed labor party of Arizona, which is out for an equitable constitution, was surprised late last night by James T. Williams, Jr., president of the Tucson Citizen Printing and Publishing company. Williams is a former United States civil service commissioner under President Taft and is here for his health. Jaynes, clerk of the district court over which Judge Campbell, also a Taft appointee, presides.

Morrison, United States district attorney, all members of the Hitchcock machine, to suppress this issue of the Voice after it came from the press and went into the United States mails, it being intended to charge that it contained scurrilous and defamatory matter.

tana at the time of the Salt Lake City

ference, but the governor made plain

program which has been arranged for
the conservation congress. The gov-
ernor said:


The states of the northwest have
by far the greater portion of the coun-
try's natural resources that are to be
conserved and this section of the

interested in every plan that tends to
the conservation of resources.

ecutives of the northwest would have
an opportunity at the St. Paul con-
servation congress to present what

western idea which epitomizes the
views of all the northwestern gover-
nors, as expressed in the conferences

ington, D. C., and which is in brief
that the national resources in very
large measure belong to the states

Governor Hughes has been driven to take up his appeals to the people by the attitude of the Woodruff-Barnes-Wadsworth group of Republican leaders in opposition to the direct primary bill and a general investigation of legislative corruption. Prepared to Battle for Measures.
But the disclosures of the Aids investigation, and later of Superintendent Hotchkiss's insurance investigation, have made great change in the Governor's views. Enactment of the Hinman-Green direct primary bill.

A thorough, broad investigation of legislative corruption.

Enactment of genuine bill for state supervision of telegraph and telephone companies.

Paul Russell Bonner, son of David Bonner, the horseman and head of the betting firm Bonner & Blackwell, 113 Hudson street—defendant—was brought here for divorce by his wife Nathalie, who was the widow James Joseph Alexander, the steamship man, when she married Mr. Bonner in 1903. Mr. Bonner was younger than his wife, having been graduated from Princeton in 1892, and he and his wife have been living at his wife's country estate, Nirvana, near Stamford.

The divorce suit became public yesterday when Supreme Court Justice Guy signed an order appointing Nathalie Duchess referee to hear it. The order did not state whether mediation and counsel for neither Mr. nor Mrs. Bonner would be required. Mr. Bonner had nothing to say, but Mrs. Bonner said that she and her husband had been separated for some time and that she was suing him for divorce.

Mr. Bonner was Nathalie's second husband, and when her husband died he left his estate in equal shares to his wife and his two children, Jerome, who was 20, and Iris, who was 15. After their mother married Mr. Bonner they continued to make their home at Nirvana.

On March 15, 1908, when Marie Joseph Alexander—Miss Violet Adelaide Oakley was announced—Miss Oakley had been employed as stenographer in Mr. Bonner's office, where his stepson met her. He had graduated from Princeton two years before. The time Mrs. Bonner said that the marriage was acceptable to her and her son, and his child, went to Nirvana to live and have been there ever since.

Public attention was directed to the Bonner in the summer of 1876 when a safe that had contained $80,000 worth of diamonds was stolen from the house while Mr. Bonner and a number of guests were asleep. The family employed detectives and called to the local police. A reward was offered, $1,000 for the jewels, but later withdrawn, and they were not recovered.

wish or intention that the inherit.
ance which he had given to his
daughter should descend from her to
his grandchildren"


This answer to the first question
covers the second one, "Is the fee
now in the grantor's son William
subject to a life estate only in the
mother?" etc.


Justice Perry concludes that the
first question should be answered in
the negative and the second in the
affirmative.

tiff and A. D. Larnach for defend
ants.

annual celebration. For more than

The commission appointed by Gov

ters in connection with the decennial
Amendment of our Constitution will
shortly publish its report, and it may
be helpful at this time to consider var
ious facts preparatory to that event.


In the first place it is to be noted that
the members of the commission are
taken from different walks of life in diff-
ferent sections of the state, and it would
be a difficult matter to pick a commis-
sion better adapted to the representation
of the sentiment of the people in this
connection than that chosen for this
present task.


The commission is composed of the
Hon. F. C. Partridge, former minister
to Venezuela, Editor Frank L. Greene
of the St. Adams Messenger, the Hon.
Allen N. Fletcher of Cavendish, who
has served in no less than four Legis-
latures, including one term as senator,

Middlebury, who is a sterling represen-
tative of Vermont's agricultural inter-
ests, and Representative N. G. Leary
of Burlington, who is a promising men-
der of the Vermont democracy.


In providing for a change in the fund
amental law of a state or nation, it must
always be borne in mind that there are
two dangers to be avoided, and one is
the possibility that amendments may
that the instrument may be so hedged
about as to render really desirable
changes a practical impossibility more
than once or twice in a generation.

law constitutional changes can be ef-

in ten years. As a matter of fact, how-

almost fifteen years from the termina-

House of Representa-tives again concur,

people for ratification at the polls. If
the amendment receives a majority of

that if the Legislature held in il-
stitution in any way our fundamental
law remains unchanged for a period of
twenty years, or practically genera-
tion. This may not be wholly unmixed
evil but the question is whether
there should not be some means of max-
imizing change in an emergency.

gestions in connection with the possible
amendment of the constitution was ap-
pointed under a law enacted in 1906
which provided among other things that
the Governor appoint a commission of

ernoon Sewing Wednesday at the

street, has invited the club for the

let Lake, Michigan.

cinnati, the house guest of Mr. and

nesday evening.

anda. In an exciting progressive

ure.

erine Turner, Emily Frank, Genevieve

night as a courtesy to Miss Nora

IRRIGATION CO.

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS: That a special meeting of the stockholders of the Southwestern Arizona Fruit and Irrigation Company, a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the Territory of Arizona, duly and regularly called and held according to the laws of Arizona, at Phoenix, Arizona, on the 2nd day of December, 1909, at the office of the corporation in Phoenix, Arizona, there being present at said meeting 29,625 shares of capital stock of said corporation out of a total issued stock of 32,591 shares outstanding, on said day, by a majority vote of the stock present as aforesaid voting in favor thereof, it was voted that the principal place of business inside the Territory of Arizona should be changed from the premises of the company in Maricopa County, Arizona, to Phoenix, Arizona; that Article VIII providing for the election of directors on the second Monday of January, be amended to the third Monday of January of each year and omitting the provision for filling vacancies, transferring this clause to the Bylaws; that Article IX relating to the officers of the Company and their duties be stricken out, transferring same to the Bylaws; that Article X be amended so as to vest in the stockholders, instead of the Board of Directors, the power to make Bylaws, rules and regulations; that the method of nomination and election of the Board of Directors be transferred to the Bylaws, and Article XII was repealed; that to accomplish all of said purposes, Articles II, VIII, IX, X & XII were amended, added to or repealed to read as follows:

Article I.—The name assumed by this corporation, and by which it shall be known, is the Southwestern Arizona Fruit and Irrigation Company, and its principal place of transacting business is and shall be in the City of Phoenix, Maricopa County, Territory of Arizona. Said corporation may transact business and have an office at Cincinnati, State of Ohio, and at such other place or places as its Board of Directors may deem convenient or advisable.

Article VIII—The affairs of this corporation shall be conducted by a Board of Directors consisting of seven stockholders, who shall be elected annually by the stockholders on the third Monday in January of each year, at the office of the Company in Arizona.

Article IX.—The Articles of Incorporation striking out therefrom Article IX.

Article X—The stockholders of this corporation shall have the power to establish bylaws and make all rules and regulations deemed expedient for the management of the affairs of this corporation and the officers thereof, not inconsistent with the Constitution and laws of the United States and the laws of Arizona.

Article XII—The Articles of Incorporation were further amended by striking out Article XII.

In Witness whereof, we, the undersigned, B. L. McGann, the president of said corporation, and E. N. Wild, the secretary of said corporation, do hereby certify that said Articles II, VIII, IX, X and XII of the Articles of Incorporation of said corporation were amended as aforesaid at said special meeting of stockholders of said corporation, by vote of more than two-thirds of the total issued stock of said corporation outstanding on said date.

Done this 18th day of December, 1909, by order of the Board of Directors and stockholders of said corporation, and with the seal of said corporation affixed this 18th day of December, 1909.

ARIZONA FRUIT & IRRIGATION CO.

By B. L. McGann, its president.

By E. N. Wild, its secretary.

State of California, County of Los Angeles, ss.

Before me, the notary public in and for the County of Los Angeles, State of California, on this 18th day of December, 1909, personally appeared B. L. McGann, known to me to be the president of the Southwestern Arizona Fruit & Irrigation Co., a corporation described in and that executed the within instrument, and acknowledged to me that the said corporation executed the above Certificate of Amendment to the Articles of Incorporation of said Company, for the purposes and considerations therein expressed.

Given under my hand and seal of office this 18th day of December, 1909.

(SEAL) J. E. OLIVER, Notary Public.

My commission expires March 8, 1913.

State of Ohio, County of Hamilton, ss.

Wild, known to me to be the secretary of the Southwestern Arizona Fruit & Irrigation Co., a corporation described in, and that executed the within instrument, and acknowledged to me that said corporation executed the above Certificate of Amendment to the Articles of Incorporation of said Company, for the purposes and considerations therein expressed.

Given under my hand and seal of office this 18th day of December, 1909.
